# Cardiac Contractility Modulation Therapy for Heart Failure: A Narrative Review

## Introduction

Heart failure (HF) remains a major global health burden, affecting an estimated 64 million people worldwide and accounting for substantial morbidity, mortality, and healthcare expenditure [1,2]. Despite advances in guideline-directed medical therapy and device-based interventions such as cardiac resynchronization therapy (CRT), a large proportion of patients remain symptomatic [3]. Notably, only about one-third of patients with HF and reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF) meet criteria for CRT, as the majority have a narrow QRS complex [4]. Cardiac contractility modulation (CCM) therapy was developed to address this therapeutic gap by enhancing myocardial contractility without the requirement for ventricular dyssynchrony [5].

## Mechanism of Action

CCM delivers high-voltage, non-excitatory electrical signals to the right ventricular septum during the absolute refractory period of the cardiac cycle [6]. Because these signals are applied when the myocardium cannot generate a new action potential, they do not provoke an additional contraction; instead, they modulate the strength of the existing contraction [7]. The proposed cellular mechanism involves enhancement of calcium handling, with increased sarcoplasmic reticulum calcium uptake and improved excitation-contraction coupling [8,9]. Experimental studies have demonstrated reversal of the fetal gene program and normalization of expression of key calcium-handling proteins such as SERCA2a and phospholamban [10,11]. These molecular changes suggest that CCM may exert favorable effects on pathological remodeling beyond its acute inotropic action [12].

## The Optimizer System

CCM is delivered via the Optimizer device, an implantable pulse generator connected to two right ventricular leads [13]. Unlike traditional inotropes, which increase myocardial oxygen consumption and are associated with adverse outcomes, CCM signals have not been shown to increase metabolic demand to a deleterious degree in clinical studies [14]. The system received CE marking in Europe and was approved by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration in 2019 for patients with NYHA class III HF, ejection fraction between 25% and 45%, and a narrow QRS who remain symptomatic despite optimal therapy [15].

## Clinical Evidence

Several randomized controlled trials have evaluated CCM. The FIX-HF-5 trial enrolled patients with NYHA class III–IV HF and an ejection fraction of 35% or less [16]. Although the primary endpoint of ventilatory anaerobic threshold was not met for the overall cohort, prespecified subgroup analyses suggested benefit in patients with ejection fraction between 25% and 45% [17]. This finding informed the design of FIX-HF-5C, which confirmed significant improvements in peak oxygen consumption, six-minute walk distance, and quality of life as measured by the Minnesota Living with Heart Failure Questionnaire [18,19].

A subsequent pooled analysis of patient-level data from CCM trials suggested a reduction in HF hospitalizations and a possible mortality signal warranting further study [20]. The FIX-HF-5C2 study evaluated a single-lead configuration and demonstrated comparable efficacy with a simplified implantation procedure [21]. Registry data and post-marketing studies, including the CCM-REG registry, have reported sustained improvements in functional class and quality of life over follow-up periods of up to two years [22,23].

Importantly, emerging evidence suggests benefit in patients with HF and preserved or mildly reduced ejection fraction, expanding the potential population [24]. Meta-analyses pooling available trials have generally confirmed improvements in exercise capacity and symptom burden, although heterogeneity in endpoints and trial size remains a limitation [25,26].

## Safety and Limitations

CCM has demonstrated an acceptable safety profile, with complication rates comparable to other implantable cardiac devices, including lead dislodgement and procedure-related events [27]. Importantly, CCM signals do not interfere with concomitant implantable cardioverter-defibrillator function when appropriate device programming is applied [28]. Nonetheless, current evidence is constrained by relatively small sample sizes, limited long-term outcome data, and a lack of adequately powered trials assessing hard endpoints such as mortality [29]. Battery longevity and the need for periodic recharging or replacement also represent practical considerations [30].

## Conclusion

CCM represents a promising device-based therapy for symptomatic HFrEF patients who are not candidates for CRT. Robust evidence supports improvements in exercise tolerance, functional capacity, and quality of life, while mechanistic data suggest favorable effects on calcium handling and reverse remodeling [8,18]. However, definitive demonstration of benefit on mortality and hospitalization through large-scale randomized trials is still needed [29]. As ongoing studies explore expanded indications—including HF with preserved ejection fraction—CCM may assume a broader role in the contemporary management of heart failure [24]. Clinicians should consider this therapy within a shared decision-making framework, weighing symptomatic benefits against current evidentiary gaps.
